questionText: Why do first-time investors start a SIP, and what are their expectations?
answer: Someone else starts them. In the survey of 27 first-time investors, 14 started because a friend, colleague, office talk or family member nudged them and 9 because of a YouTube or Instagram creator; only 4 did their own research. The public corpus shows the same pull of creators. Expectations are that a SIP is hassle-free and automatic, and often that it is safe or that a specific return will come (“will I get 12%?”). The first time the payment plumbing shows through, that expectation breaks.

questionText: How does behavior/emotion evolve from Month 1 through Month 8–12?
answer: Before starting: curious and cautious. At setup: alarm at the mandate ceiling (19 of 27 survey respondents were thrown by a limit far above their SIP). Months 2–4 are the danger window: 22 of the 32 survey and interview records place their decisive moment there, nearly always the first failed debit, followed by a bank penalty, an unexplained status, or no way to retry. Emotion moves from worry to embarrassment or panic, then to inaction: the SIP is paused, left “to sort out later”, or silently lapses. People who get past month 4 without a failure keep running. The data still has no records from months 9–12.

questionText: What triggers a decision to pause, skip, or cancel?
answer: The first failed instalment. 20 of 27 survey respondents had an instalment fail, get skipped or get paused, and only 2 of those 20 are still active; all 7 who never had one are still running. The failure itself usually comes from the SIP date landing before salary or a low balance, a bank-side or UPI glitch, or a reason the investor never learns (5 of 27). What turns it into a stop is the bank's bounce charge (₹295–450, often felt more than the instalment), no in-app explanation, and no way to pay that month. Early flat or negative returns trigger pauses too, and money stuck “in progress” triggers cancellations.

questionText: What do users monitor in the app, and how often?
answer: They reconcile bank SMS against the app around debit dates: was money taken, and did units appear? 5 of 27 survey respondents saw units more than 3 days after the debit, and in interviews that gap was read as money lost. Outside debit days most don't watch at all, which is why a failed instalment can go unnoticed for two months. Continuers describe a light monthly check of the portfolio.

questionText: What inside-app elements create confusion or misplaced blame?
answer: The autopay screen showing ₹15,000 or ₹25,000 for a ₹500–2,500 SIP (70% of survey respondents); status labels like “Mandate Expired”, “Payment Initiated” or “In Progress” that then fail silently; a warning icon with no action; and no button to retry or pay the missed month. Bank bounce charges are blamed on the investment app, and support calling them “not our problem” deepens the distrust.

questionText: What outside-app workarounds do investors use?
answer: The main escape hatch is revoking the autopay mandate directly in a UPI app (PhonePe, Google Pay or BHIM) to stop further bounce charges, which ends the SIP without the investment app seeing a cancellation. Others search Google, YouTube or Reddit, ask a friend or roommate (one switched to a net-banking mandate that way), or ask creators in YouTube comments. The most common response is no response: 13 of 27 survey respondents did nothing, and none of those 13 are still active.

questionText: Are there different churn patterns across investor segments?
answer: Income type matters most: neither freelancer in the survey is still active and both students struggled, because fixed-date automatic debits don't fit irregular income. Among salaried first-jobbers 4 of 13 are active versus 4 of 10 with 2+ years' experience. Creator-led starters fare worst (2 of 9 active) next to friend- or colleague-led ones (3 of 10). In the public corpus, Hinglish speakers are over-represented in mandate and debit confusion. The survey is small, so treat these as directions to test, not rates.

questionText: What consistent unmet needs surface across the corpus?
answer: (1) A plain note at setup that the mandate amount is a ceiling, not a charge. (2) A SIP date chosen around salary day, plus a balance reminder the day before the debit. (3) A same-day “retry / pay this month now” after a failed debit. (4) A proactive alert when an instalment fails, with the reason in plain language instead of jargon. (5) Reassurance on who charges the bounce fee and that a SIP bounce doesn't touch the credit score. (6) A clear unit-allotment timeline. (7) Easy pause and resume. (8) SEBI-safe education for “which fund / how much return” questions.
